nameStory: The old-man-of-the-woods gets its whimsical name from its distinctive appearance - the dark, shaggy scales covering its cap look remarkably like scraggly gray hair or whiskers of an elderly forest hermit. When you spot one peeking up through the leaf litter, it's easy to imagine a grumpy old woodsman's head poking out of the ground!
description: Old-man-of-the-woods is one of New England's most distinctive mushrooms, impossible to mistake once you've seen one. This bolete has a dark gray to blackish cap covered in soft, fluffy scales that give it an unmistakably shaggy appearance. Instead of gills underneath, it has tiny pores like other boletes, and the entire mushroom tends to turn black when bruised or with age. It's a medium-sized mushroom that can grow several inches across.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Dark gray to black with distinctive soft, woolly scales that feel like cotton or felt when touched - this shaggy texture is unlike any other mushroom in our region

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: White to gray pores underneath instead of gills, turning darker with age and bruising black when pressed

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Gray to blackish stem that's often scaly like the cap and feels firm but not woody

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: The entire mushroom gradually turns black when handled or cut, and old specimens become completely black

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, earthy mushroom smell without any strong or unpleasant odors

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Black spore print - place cap pore-side down on white paper overnight to see this diagnostic feature

habitat: Look for old-man-of-the-woods in mixed hardwood and coniferous forests throughout New England, especially under oaks, maples, and pines. They form partnerships with tree roots (mycorrhizal relationships) and prefer well-drained, acidic soils typical of our northeastern woodlands. You'll often find them scattered individually or in small groups along woodland trails and in mature forest areas.

seasonality.spring: Not typically found in spring - the mushroom season hasn't begun yet for this species.
seasonality.summer: Begins appearing in mid to late summer, especially after warm, soaking rains when forest soils are thoroughly moistened.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding old-man-of-the-woods, fruiting regularly through early to mid-fall until hard frosts arrive. This is when you're most likely to spot their distinctive shaggy caps.
seasonality.winter: No fruiting bodies present - the fungus survives underground as thread-like mycelia connected to tree roots.

funFact: Old-man-of-the-woods is one of the few boletes that produces black spores instead of the typical brown or olive colors - if you've ever seen mysterious black powder on leaves beneath these mushrooms, you've discovered their spore deposits!
confusionNotes: The shaggy, scaly cap makes this virtually impossible to confuse with any other mushroom in New England - no other species has this distinctive cotton-ball texture combined with pores instead of gills. Memory trick: if it looks like it needs a haircut, it's probably old-man-of-the-woods!
contextualKnowledge: This mushroom has had several scientific names over the years, including Strobilomyces floccopus, which you might see in older field guides. The genus name Strobilomyces comes from Greek words meaning 'cone fungus' referring to the scale-covered cap that resembles a pine cone.
compareHints: Old-man-of-the-woods is quite different from its relative Strobilomyces confusus, which is much rarer in our region and has a smoother cap surface without the distinctive shaggy scales. Compared to other boletes in the family, this species stands out dramatically with its dark coloration and unique scaly texture - most other boletes have smooth, often colorful caps and don't turn black when bruised.
